title: India's 'own GPS', which new ISRO satellite can restore
syllabus: GS3 › Awareness in the field of space; Indigenisation of technology and developing new technology; Security challenges and their management in border areas · GS4 › Foundational values: courage of conviction, fortitude
summary: ISRO is launching NVS-03 to restore NavIC, India's regional navigation system, which stopped giving location data after repeated satellite failures.
ideas: Strategic sovereignty in space: NavIC (the working name of IRNSS) is a seven-satellite system covering India and up to 1,500 km around it. India is the only country with a regional navigation system; the four global ones are GPS, GLONASS, Galileo and BeiDou.
NavIC gives India its own positioning, navigation and timing, so it need not depend on foreign systems such as GPS in a crisis.

Serving citizens and soldiers: when fully working, NavIC gives the public accuracy of up to 10 metres and a restricted, fee-based service to users such as the military. It covers the Indian landmass better than GPS, whose signals reach India at an angle and struggle in valleys and forests.
As a dual-use system, NavIC serves both public navigation and the armed forces, with better coverage in India's valleys and forests than GPS.

Imported parts were the weak link: six of the 11 navigation satellites launched since 2013 failed, mainly because of defective imported atomic clocks. Replacements also failed: IRNSS-1H's heat shield did not open and NVS-02's propulsion failed. The Centre told Parliament this year that the system no longer gave position data.
NavIC's failures show that a strategic system is only as sovereign as its least indigenous component.

Learning from failure: from NVS-01, satellites carry Indian-made atomic clocks with a 12-year life (up from 10), and propulsion systems now get more thorough checks. The new L1 frequency, the band GPS mostly uses, lets NavIC work with other systems and run on low-power chips in smartwatches.
By building its own atomic clocks and tightening checks after failures, ISRO turned setbacks into a stronger second generation of NavIC.

examples: Defective imported clocks caused most of NavIC's satellite failures
NavIC's imported atomic clocks failing is a textbook case of strategic risk from critical imports.
New-generation satellites add the L1 band used by low-power wearable chips
With the L1 band, NavIC reaches everyday devices such as smartwatches.
After clock, heat-shield and propulsion failures, ISRO built clocks at home, tightened checks and launched again
ISRO's return to launch after repeated failures shows institutional courage: owning mistakes and persisting.

practice.q: Why does India need its own regional navigation system when global systems such as GPS are freely available? Explain.

answer.t: NavIC, the seven-satellite Indian Regional Navigation Satellite System, makes India the only country with its own regional navigation system.

pts.t: Foreign systems can be switched off or degraded in a conflict; an indigenous system removes this signal-denial risk.
A restricted, encrypted service supports the armed forces in guidance, troop movement and border surveillance.
pts.ex: NavIC's fee-based restricted service for select users.

pts.t: GPS signals reach India at an angle and weaken in valleys and forests; NavIC is designed for the Indian landmass.

pts.t: Precise positioning helps rescue operations and guides fishermen at sea.
Transport, logistics, surveying and large construction projects need reliable positioning.

pts.ex: Indian-made atomic clocks from NVS-01 onwards.

pts.t: Learn from the imported clock failures; build key components at home.
Plan replacements ahead of satellites' end of life.
Encourage NavIC-enabled chips in phones and wearables through the L1 band.

answer.t: A fully restored NavIC would turn India's space capability into everyday strategic security.
